title: Governor of Alabama

context.text: Open seat: Republican Gov. Kay Ivey is term-limited. The race is a rematch of the 2020 U.S. Senate contest between Tommy Tuberville and Doug Jones.
Republican primary (May 19): U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville won with about 85% of the vote in unofficial results from Ken McFeeters and Will Santivasci; Lt. Gov. Will Ainsworth had declined to run.
Democratic primary (May 19): former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones won with about 78% in unofficial results, ahead of Will Boyd, 2022 nominee Yolanda Flowers and three others.

A lawsuit challenging whether Tuberville meets Alabama's residency requirement was dismissed by a Montgomery judge for lack of jurisdiction in July; the plaintiffs appealed to the Alabama Supreme Court.

The Alabama Secretary of State's August 26 certifications list only Tuberville (Republican) and Jones (Democrat) for governor, and the certified independent candidates include no one for governor. Independents Ronald Burnette Jr. and Darren Knight are reported as declared write-in candidates; write-in candidates do not appear as printed names on the ballot.

candidates.name: Tommy Tuberville
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Republican primary; Alabama elects its lieutenant governor separately. Endorsed by President Trump.

summary.text: Tommy Tuberville is Alabama's senior U.S. senator and a former college football head coach, including at Auburn University from 1999 to 2008. First elected in 2020 when he defeated Sen. Doug Jones, he is running for governor on an 'Alabama First Agenda' of cutting taxes and government waste, expanding school choice, protecting Second Amendment rights and tougher border enforcement.

background.text: Born in Camden, Arkansas; earned a B.S. in physical education from Southern State College (now Southern Arkansas University) in 1976.
Head football coach at Ole Miss (1995–1998), Auburn (1999–2008), Texas Tech (2010–2012) and Cincinnati (2013–2016).
Elected to the U.S. Senate in 2020, defeating incumbent Democrat Doug Jones; his first political campaign.

priorities.text: Cutting taxes, reducing government waste and bringing manufacturing jobs back to Alabama.
Expanding school choice and supporting workforce-development schools, including trades-focused high schools.
Strong border enforcement and deportation of illegal immigrants with criminal records; opposition to taxpayer-funded abortion; support for farmers, the defense sector and veterans.

positions.summary: His campaign agenda lists expanding school choice.
Promises strong border enforcement and deportation of people in the country illegally who have criminal records.
Opposes taxpayer-funded abortion; said on primary night 'I'm running against people that believe in killing the unborn.'
positions.quote: I'm running against people that believe in killing the unborn.

record.text: Voted yea on H.R. 1, the budget reconciliation bill (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), which passed the Senate 50–50 with the Vice President breaking the tie.
Secured funding for the expansion of the Wiregrass Public Safety Center, a law-enforcement training facility in Dothan, and has introduced veterans-related bills that became law.

candidates.name: Doug Jones
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Democratic primary with about 78% of the vote in unofficial results.

summary.text: Doug Jones is a lawyer and former U.S. senator, who served from 2018 to 2021 after winning a 2017 special election, and U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Alabama from 1997 to 2001. He is running on expanding Medicaid, eliminating the state grocery tax and taxes on tips and overtime, raising the minimum wage, a one-year moratorium on data centers, and a citizen ballot-initiative process.

background.text: Born in Fairfield, Alabama; graduated from the University of Alabama (1976) and Cumberland School of Law at Samford University (1979).

Staff counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee, Assistant U.S. Attorney (1980–1984), private practice, then U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Alabama (1997–2001), where he prosecuted two Ku Klux Klan members for the 1963 Birmingham church bombing and indicted Eric Rudolph.
Won a 2017 special election for the U.S. Senate seat vacated by Jeff Sessions and lost re-election to Tommy Tuberville in 2020.

priorities.text: Expanding Medicaid 'one way or another,' protecting rural hospitals and improving maternal, infant and mental health care.
Eliminating the state grocery tax and state taxes on tips and overtime; raising the minimum wage; making child care and housing more affordable.
A one-year moratorium on data centers, a citizen-led ballot initiative process, a statewide vote on a lottery, and constitutional protections for IVF and contraception.

positions.summary: Says Alabama should expand Medicaid, calling it 'not a handout, it's a hand up.'
positions.quote: Medicaid expansion is not a handout, it's a hand up.

positions.summary: Has called for raising Alabama's minimum wage.

record.text: Voted guilty on Article I of the Articles of Impeachment against President Donald Trump, which failed 48–52 in the Senate.
Voted yea on overriding the President's veto of S.J. Res. 68, a joint resolution directing removal of U.S. forces from hostilities against Iran not authorized by Congress; the veto was sustained.

researchNotes: Ballotpedia was blocked in this environment, so candidate details come from Alabama Reflector, WSFA, 256 Today and Wikipedia; the slate was confirmed against the Alabama Secretary of State's August 26 certifications of Republican, Democratic and independent candidates (scanned PDFs, read visually), which list only Tuberville and Jones for governor; no minor-party certification was located. Alabama elects its lieutenant governor separately, so there are no running mates. Neither campaign site could be loaded for Tuberville; his 'Alabama First Agenda' is described via 256 Today's report of his announcement, so his positions are thinly sourced. Jones's campaign site loaded only as a shell, so his platform comes from his July 27 policy speech as reported by Alabama Reflector and Tuscaloosa Thread. Senate floor votes are listed from senate.gov; broader Senate votes for Tuberville are expected to be added later by script.
